title: Nuclear Asteroid Defense: New LLNL 3D Simulations Reveal 98% Destruction Rate
byline: Сollin Rugg View all posts by Сollin Rugg
excerpt: New 3D simulations show a nuclear device could neutralize an incoming asteroid, with up to 98% of material damaged and 97% blown past escape velocity.
content:
A targeted nuclear detonation can shatter a hazardous asteroid heading toward Earth, with cutting-edge 3D models proving that roughly 98% of target rock sustains structural damage while 97% is accelerated past escape velocity. Published in The Planetary Science Journal, research led by the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) reveals how intense X-ray bursts can tear apart a massive celestial body before it ever reaches our atmosphere.

Planetary defence experts have spent years exploring methods to safeguard the globe from rogue space rocks. While gentle kinetic nudges offer a viable route when detected decades in advance, late-stage emergency threats require an entirely different tier of delivered energy to prevent catastrophic impacts.

The Physics of Extreme Deflection

When an asteroid is caught on a collision course with Earth, scientists evaluate two distinct emergency responses: deflection or outright disruption. Deflection introduces a slight velocity change, causing the intact rock to bypass the planet safely, whereas disruption fragments the target into harmless debris.

The practical baseline for kinetic redirection was demonstrated in 2022 when NASA collided its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) probe directly into the small asteroid moon Dimorphos. While that spacecraft relied strictly on physical momentum transfer, nuclear mitigation acts as the primary option when facing much larger targets or drastically shortened warning times.

“These simulations give us a much more detailed picture of how an asteroid may respond to a nuclear mitigation attempt,” said Isaiah Santistevan, who led the study. “Being able to model damage, fracture and material motion in three dimensions is an important step toward improving our ability to evaluate planetary defense options.”

Unlike standard science-fiction tropes, the device does not rely on a conventional atmospheric blast shockwave. Instead, high-energy X-rays emitted by a stand-off nuclear detonation strike the asteroid’s surface, rapidly heating and vaporising exterior rock. This explosive outgassing creates a violent reactive kick that either pushes the core off course or fractures it into expanding fragments.


LLNL simulations explore nuclear mitigation of asteroid threats

Benchmarking with Advanced Hydrodynamics

To accurately recreate the mechanics of high-velocity destruction, LLNL researchers employed their proprietary Spheral code. This software platform specialises in tracking extreme physical phenomena, including complex material fracture, fragmentation, and hydrodynamic damage evolution under explosive loads.

Before launching full 3D models, the research team validated the framework against established benchmarks by running more than 1,500 one-dimensional simulations alongside LLNL’s proven Ares code. The cross-checked data yielded close alignment, providing the mathematical confidence needed to subject irregularly shaped, 160-metre (525-foot) rocky bodies to simulated atomic bursts.

Shattering a 160-Metre Asteroid

The research team evaluated three complex disruption scenarios across variable detonation stand-off distances and distinct fracture thresholds. Across two of these setups, the simulated rocky mass displayed undeniable markers of total physical collapse.

In the primary run, roughly 98% of the asteroid material experienced complete structural failure, destroying its cohesion. Simultaneously, 97% of the shattered fragments exceeded the asteroid’s gravitational escape velocity, dispersing outward in opposite directions to prevent post-blast reassembly.

The simulations also uncovered a counter-intuitive principle regarding nuclear weapon placement. Detonating a warhead further back from the asteroid surface deposited lower total raw energy, yet it achieved far wider structural fracture because the X-ray footprint covered a much broader surface area.

“What’s encouraging is that we’re seeing the asteroid sustain extensive damage while material is also moving fast enough to escape its gravitational pull,” Santistevan explained.

A widespread public misconception suggests that detonating an asteroid simply replaces a single cannonball with an equally deadly cloud of radioactive buckshot. For complete planetary protection, rigorous planetary defence safety standards require all remaining fragments to measure less than 10 metres (33 feet) across so they burn up entirely during atmospheric entry.

Pushing Supercomputing to the Millisecond

Capturing the complete, multi-day lifecycle of shattered debris requires enormous computational investment. LLNL’s longest continuous calculation engaged 1,680 parallel processors for 59 straight days, yet that massive computational effort simulated only 145 milliseconds of real-world physical time.

Because the calculations stopped well before the clouds of dust and stone settled, researchers intend to accelerate future runtimes and test looser “rubble-pile” compositions. Confirming that fragments do not coalesce requires tracking these trajectories over longer intervals, blending supercomputing models with controlled laboratory hypervelocity impacts.
